text: Three questions about the chapters, then the first step of your own writing. When a question asks for evidence, use Isaac's own words. In the Writer's Workshop you are only making a list today. Pick moments you can still feel.
Read Chapters one and two in your book. Keep your reading lens in mind as you go. When you finish, do the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.
Read Chapters 1 and 2 in your book. Keep your reading lens in mind as you go. When you finish, do the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

This book starts with a boy who says something no narrator should be able to say. He is a ghost. Then he says he is not a ghost yet. Hold on to both of those. Today you meet Isaac, his family, and his dog Jumper, in the Choctaw Nation in 1830. Keep one question with you: what does Isaac know that you don't?

Two word parts run through this whole book. One is about remembering. One is about writing. Isaac is doing both. Try to find them before the page tells you. When you get to the river game, say each word slowly and listen for where your voice stops.
Three questions about Chapters 3 and 4, and then a draft of your own moment. Pick one moment from your list. Write it from the inside, with I, the way Isaac does.

Read Chapters three and four in your book. These are hard chapters. Isaac sees more visions, and then something happens that is not a vision at all. Take your time. When you finish, do the Virtue Watch, then the Read Like a Writer box.

Read Chapters 3 and 4 in your book. These are hard chapters. Isaac sees more visions, and then something happens that is not a vision at all. Take your time. When you finish, do the Virtue Watch, then the Read Like a Writer box.

Last lesson, Isaac saw something nobody else could see. Today you find out what it meant. Start with the warm-up. The DOL sentence comes straight from Chapter 4, and it moves. Then read the poem and listen for who is talking in it.
Today you match each word to its root, and you read this week's words in sentences from the book. In the river game, say each word slowly and listen for where your voice stops.
Three questions, and then you revise. Add one inside detail to your draft: something you saw, heard, felt, or thought. One detail can change a whole paragraph.
Read Chapters five and six in your book. Then reread one passage, the way What Good Readers Do asks. When you finish, do the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.
Read Chapters 5 and 6 in your book. Then reread one passage, the way What Good Readers Do asks. When you finish, do the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.
Isaac's family is in the swamp now, with almost nothing. Watch how the people work together. Start with the warm-up sentence about Old Man and his blanket.
Today you build appositives yourself and use your roots to work out words you have never seen. The river game has root stones now. Tap only the letters of the root.
Three questions, and the last one looks back over the whole week. Then write the clean, final version of your moment, and submit your work.
Read Chapter seven in your book. When you finish, think about the whole week. What has Isaac's voice shown you that a history book could not? Then pick the bravest moment of the week in Virtue Watch.
Read Chapter 7 in your book. When you finish, think about the whole week. What has Isaac's voice shown you that a history book could not? Then pick the bravest moment of the week in Virtue Watch.
This is the last day of the week, and Chapter 7 has a surprise in it. It is funny. Start with the warm-up. In the poem, think about the speaker, the voice inside the poem.
Last day with these roots. Build the words from their pieces, then use this week's words in your own sentences. Finish your river crossing too.

Read the opening of the book out loud. Isaac is talking right to you, so read it the way he would say it. Slow down on the warning at the end of the first paragraph. When it sounds smooth, record yourself and turn it in.

Three questions about Chapter 8, then the first step of a new piece of writing. When a question asks why, give the reason and the words from the book that show it. In the Writer's Workshop you are only planning today. A few notes are enough.

Read Chapter 8 of How I Became a Ghost in your book. Keep your reading lens in mind. Watch how Isaac's family meets new people on the road, and listen for what Mister Jonah tells Isaac about the blankets. When you finish, do the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

Isaac's family has been hiding in the swamp. In Chapter 8 they have to decide whether to stay or go, and what to take with them. Before you read, think about what people carry when they leave home. What someone holds on to can show how they see the world. That is your reading lens this week.

Two roots this week. One means life. One means breath. Long ago, people thought those were almost the same thing. Look for them in words you already know. Then three endings that turn a word into a describing word. In the footprint game, say each word out loud before you pick an ending.

Three questions about Chapter 9, then a first draft. Write three to five sentences about the conflict you planned. Let the tension build, and do not solve the problem yet. Copy your work into Canvas when you finish.

Read Chapter 9 in your book. Watch what Isaac promises, and what he does the next morning to keep that promise. Then read the Read Like a Writer sentence and notice how Isaac lets you inside his head. Finish with the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

Isaac's family is walking with Gabe, Ruth and their little girl, Nita. Nita is five, and she has something to ask Isaac. The poem today has an I in it, but that I is not the poet. Keep that in mind. A voice in a poem or a story can belong to someone the writer made.

You met the life root and the breath root. Now decide which one is hiding in each word. Some words carry both ideas. Then sort the describing words by their endings. Find the smaller word inside first. Then the footprint game has six new words to build.

Three questions about Chapter 10. The last one looks back across Chapters 8, 9 and 10. Then revise your draft. Read it with the checklist first and fix what it shows you. Then add one sentence where everything is about to break.

Read Chapter 10 in your book. It is a hard chapter. Read the part where Isaac's father speaks to him twice: once for the story, and once to hear how his father says it. Then try the Read Like a Writer box, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

Chapter 10 is the coldest day of the walk. Mister Jonah warned Isaac it would be hard. As you read, notice the moment Isaac almost gives up, and the words that bring him back. Today you will reread one line closely. One sentence can hold a whole way of seeing the world.

Today you put the roots to work. In Spelling, the words are new. Build each describing word in your head before you place it. If the base ends in a silent e, check whether it stays or goes. The footprint game works the same way.

Three questions about Chapter 11, then your final piece. Write your conflict scene in five to seven sentences, and end while the tension is still high. Then write one sentence about what Isaac taught you about rising action. Copy your work and paste it into Canvas.

Read Chapter 11 in your book. Go slowly. Notice Nita's gift to Isaac, and how Isaac's family and friends take care of each other. Then put the week together with your lens: pick two people and compare how they see the same road. Finish with the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

This is the last day of the week. In Chapter 11, Nita gives Isaac a gift, and the chapter ends with a hard loss. Read it slowly. The poem today is spoken by a mother to her son. Listen for how her advice sounds like the words Isaac's father said in Chapter 10.

Last day with life and breath. Today you explain why one idea needed two roots. In Spelling, the words change in different ways when an ending is added. Sometimes a silent e drops. Sometimes the base changes more. Sometimes nothing changes. Look closely at the base each time.

Read this part of Chapter 10 out loud. First Isaac tells what happens. Then his father speaks, calm and sure. Let your voice change for the father's words, and give each short sentence its own beat. When it sounds smooth, record yourself and turn it in.

Three questions about Chapter 12, then the plan for a theme paragraph. A theme is a big idea the book shows, like courage or justice. Today you only pick one and note two pieces of evidence. Copy your work into Canvas when you finish.

Read Chapter 12 of How I Became a Ghost in your book. Nita's ghost comes to Isaac with a request: find her sister. Watch what happens when Isaac asks Gabe about it, and notice what makes the tension grow. Then do the Virtue Watch and the Read Like a Writer box.

Nita has died, and her family carries her on the walk. In Chapter 12, Isaac learns that Nita's family has a secret. Before you read, think about secrets. When is it right to keep one, and when is it right to tell? Your reading lens this week is how a story's pressure builds.

Two new roots this week, and both are about feeling. One leans toward emotion. One leans toward the senses. Then listen to long words. When a word grows, its strongest beat can move. In the council fire game, say each word out loud and tap the beat you say the strongest.

Three questions about Chapter 13, then the first sentences of your theme paragraph. Start with a sentence that names the theme. Then add one piece of evidence from the book, and connect them with a complex sentence.

Read Chapter 13 in your book. Listen for Gabe's secret and Isaac's secret, and notice why each one was kept. Then look at how Tingle orders the events in the Read Like a Writer sentence. Finish with the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

In Chapter 13, two secrets come out around one campfire, and then someone new arrives in the dark. The poem today is about choosing a road. Look at where its lines break. A line break can make a reader wait, the same way a writer builds tension.

Today you decide which feeling root is in each word: the one for emotion, or the one for the senses. Then sort words by where the stress falls. Say each word twice, leaning on a different beat each time. Only one way sounds right.
Three questions about Chapter 14. The last one connects three secrets from Chapters 12, 13 and 14. Then revise your theme paragraph with the checklist, and add a second piece of evidence.

Read Chapter 14 in your book. Joseph tells his story in order, from the hunt to the cave. Follow each step. Then try the Read Like a Writer box, where one sentence skips a whole night, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

In Chapter 14, Joseph tells Isaac his story: how he was caught, and how he got away. He tells it calmly, but a lot happens. Today you will reread part of it and put the events in order. Notice which event made the next one possible.

Put the feeling roots to work today. Then the spelling words: when a vowel is too quiet to hear, say a related word where that beat is strong. The vowel comes back. The council fire game uses the same trick.

Three questions about Chapter 15, then your finished theme paragraph: five to seven sentences, with a topic sentence, two pieces of evidence and a closing. Then one sentence about the hardest part. Copy your work and paste it into Canvas.

Read Chapter 15 in your book. Watch how the Choctaw Council welcomes Isaac, and listen to what the council leader asks him. Then put the week together with your lens: where did the danger change? Finish with the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

This is the last day of the week. In Chapter 15, Isaac learns that Choctaw leaders travel with the walkers in a council wagon, and a ghost gives him a plan. The poem today never names what it describes. Let each line break show you a little more.

Last day with the feeling roots. Explain the difference between feeling with someone and feeling from inside their experience. In spelling, the vowel you cannot hear hides in the quiet beat. Find a relative that makes it loud.

Read this part of Chapter 12 out loud. Isaac is walking blind through the snow, and his mind tells him a frightening story. Let the tension build as the icicle waits. Whisper the first no, and shout the second. When it sounds smooth, record yourself and turn it in.

Three questions about Chapter 16. Then a new piece of writing begins. This week you will go back to a story you wrote and make the pictures in it stronger. Today you only choose three moments to work on.

Read Chapter 16 of How I Became a Ghost in your book. Watch what the boys tell the council leader, and what the council decides to do about Naomi. Then do the Read Like a Writer box and the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

In Chapter 16, a council leader catches Isaac and Joseph talking by the creek at night, and the Choctaw Council learns about Naomi. Your reading lens this week is theme. Watch for things that come back in the story, like blankets and footprints. Each time, ask what they mean now.

Two roots this week, and both are about sight. One means see. One means look. Then words that sound the same but are spelled differently. A spell checker will not catch them. In the spyglass game, find the root first, then the meaning.

Three questions about Chapter 17, then your first revision. Take the first moment from your plan. Add one detail you can see, hear, smell or feel, and one comparison. Show the old version first, then the new one.

Read Chapter 17 in your book. Watch how Isaac spends the day with his family, and what he says when it is time to go. Then read the Read Like a Writer sentence about a council leader, and finish with the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

In Chapter 17, Isaac goes back to visit his family. The poem today repeats one line, and a new picture follows it each time. Watch what the second picture adds. Then think about something that keeps coming back in Isaac's story.

Today you decide which root each word carries: see, or look. Then sort the sound alike words by the job they do. Does the word show who owns something, name a thing, or squeeze two words together? Then five new words in the spyglass.

Three questions about Chapter 18. The last one looks back across Chapters 16, 17 and 18. Then revise with the checklist, and work on your second moment. Choose a comparison that fits the feeling of the moment.

Read Chapter 18 in your book. Isaac says good-bye to his mother, and then the chapter changes everything. Notice the words from his father that Isaac remembers. Then try the Read Like a Writer box, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

Chapter 18 is the hardest chapter in the book. It is the chapter Isaac told you about on the first page. Read it slowly. If it feels heavy, that is all right. Today you will reread one passage and trace an idea back to where you first met it.

Put the sight roots to work today. Then the sound alike words again, sorted a new way: is the word a thing, an action, or two words squeezed? Say it in a sentence to check. Then five new words in the spyglass.

Three questions about Chapter 19, then your final revised story: five to seven sentences with at least one detail you can sense and one comparison. Then one sentence about what imagery adds. Copy your work and paste it into Canvas.

Read Chapter 19 in your book. Watch what Isaac discovers in the soldiers' camp, and listen to what Naomi says when he whispers her name. Then put the week together with your lens: name the theme. Finish with the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

This is the last day of the week. In Chapter 19, Isaac learns what he can and cannot do as a ghost, and he goes looking for Naomi. The poem today asks the same question twice. Notice how you can know something is there, even when you cannot see it.

Last day with the sight roots. Explain the difference between looking and seeing. Then the academic pairs that trip up even grown writers: affect and effect, principal and principle. Then the last five words in the spyglass.

Read this part of Chapter 19 out loud. Isaac has just realized the soldiers cannot hurt him. Let that surprise come through in your voice. Then slow down as he watches the young man by the fire, and laugh at yourself with Isaac when he figures out who it is. When it sounds smooth, record yourself and turn it in.
Three questions about Chapter 20. Then a new piece of writing begins: a paragraph about the novel. Today you only plan. Choose a topic, write your claim, and find two pieces of evidence.

Read Chapter 20 in your book. Watch what Naomi does to stay strong, and what goes wrong with Isaac's plan. This chapter is hard. Take it slowly. Then do the Read Like a Writer box and the Virtue Watch.

In Chapter 20, Isaac finally reaches Naomi, and the chapter takes a hard turn. Your reading lens this week is figurative language. Watch for comparisons, where one thing is described as another. Each time, ask what the picture makes you feel.

Two roots this week mean light. One came from Latin, one from Greek. Then long words about books, built from parts you already know. In the lantern game, build each word from its parts, and watch the lantern light up.
Three questions about Chapter 21. Then write the full draft of your paragraph: a claim, two pieces of evidence with your explanation, and a closing sentence. Use at least one transition word.

Read Chapter 21 in your book. Track what the panther does, one action at a time, and how each one helps Naomi get away. Then try the Read Like a Writer sentence about the fire, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

In Chapter 21, Joseph becomes the panther again, and a dog surprises everyone. The poem today is about a tiger burning bright. Watch which pictures Blake gives you, and listen for fire in the chapter too.
Today, decide whether each light word came from Latin or from Greek. Then sort long book words by the root at their center. Then four new lanterns to light.
Three questions about Chapter 22. Then revise your paragraph with the checklist. Check every he, she and they. Improve one transition. Cut words you do not need. Show one sentence before and after.

Read Chapter 22 in your book. Watch who welcomes Naomi, and why their wagon is the safest place for her. Then reread the thunderbolt sentence in the Read Like a Writer box, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

Chapter 22 takes Naomi somewhere nobody would think to look. Part of it explains how some Choctaw women cared for people who had died. Read it calmly. Today you will reread one sentence and notice how it is built.
Put the light words to work today. Then try book words you have never studied. Break each one into its parts, and work out the meaning before anyone tells you. Then four new lanterns.

Three questions about Chapter 23. Then write the final version of your paragraph, with every pronoun clear. Last, explain how a summary and an analysis are different. Copy your work and paste it into Canvas.

Read Chapter 23 in your book. Watch how the women's plan works, and what the ghosts tell the boys. Then put the week together with your lens: choose the picture that carries the most. Finish with the Virtue Watch.

This is the last day of the week. In Chapter 23, the plan to hide Naomi goes into action, and the three boys get a visit they will never forget. The poem today is about snowy woods at night. Listen for how quiet it feels.
Last day with the light roots. Explain why writers use light to talk about understanding. Then build words of your own from Greek and Latin parts, and light the last lanterns of the week.

Read this part of Chapter 23 out loud. Start slowly, like the wind and the sleet. Let Joseph's words shiver. Pause when the branch cracks, then let the last line land. You heard it on the first page of the book. When it sounds smooth, record yourself.

Three questions about Chapter 24. Then your final writing piece of the unit begins. Today you only plan. Choose your strongest writing from the last five weeks, and decide what to keep, what to cut, and how to begin.
Read Chapter 24 in your book. Watch what Leader vows, and how his own soldiers react. Then try the Read Like a Writer sentence about the wagon fire, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

In Chapter 24, Isaac spends a whole night awake while everyone else sleeps, and by morning Leader has made a dangerous vow. Your reading skill this week is summarizing. A good summary keeps only the events the story could not do without.

Two roots this week are about speaking. Voc, or voke, means voice or call. Dict means say. Then a year of spelling patterns, all in one sort. In the game, read each line and choose the word that fits the blank.
Three questions about Chapter 25. Then write the first full draft of your final piece. Use what you have learned this year: strong verbs, clear pronouns, and sentences that show how ideas connect.
Read Chapter 25 in your book. After each big moment, say in one sentence what changed. Then write your own summary sentence in the Read Like a Writer box, and finish with the Virtue Watch.
Chapter 25 is called A Day of Death, but read closely: by the end of the chapter, who has actually died? Today's poem is a sonnet about a statue that speaks. Notice how its shape fits its voice.
Today, decide whether each word carries voc and voke, calling out, or dict, saying and declaring. Then sort words by the rule that explains their spelling. Then three new lines to finish in the game.
Three questions about Chapter 26. Then revise your draft with the checklist: strong verbs, a combined sentence, clear pronouns, and at least one transition word. Star your three best sentences.

Read Chapter 26 in your book. Watch what Ruth does when Leader demands her little girl, and what stops Pointy Nose. Then try the Read Like a Writer sentence that begins with Instead, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

In Chapter 26, Leader reaches Isaac's family, still hunting for Naomi. Ruth answers him without arguing at all. Today you will reread one passage and sum it up in two sentences: what happened, and what it meant.
Put the speaking roots to work today. Then learn how transition words, like but, because and instead, show how ideas connect. Then check your own draft, one spelling pattern at a time.
Three questions about Chapter 27. Then write the final version of your piece, clean and complete. Add one sentence about what it shows about you as a writer. Copy your work and paste it into Canvas.
Read Chapter 27 in your book. It ends in a frightening moment, so take it slowly. Then put the book together so far: who Isaac has become, what he faces, and what being a ghost lets him see.

This is the last day of the week. In Chapter 27, the soldiers reach the bonepickers' wagon, where Naomi is still hiding. Today's poem was written in the shape of a gravestone. Listen for how calm it is.
Last day with the speaking roots. Match words to the roots you have collected all year. Then explain a spelling pattern the way you would teach it to a friend, and finish the last lines of the game.
Read this part of Chapter 24 out loud. Let the long list in the third sentence roll along without stopping. Then slow down while Isaac watches Joseph sleep. When it sounds smooth, record yourself.
Three questions about Chapter 28. Then plan your source comparison. You need a claim, one detail from the novel, one line from a real source, and your reasoning. Today you only plan.
Read Chapter 28 in your book. Watch the panther and the wolf, and listen to what Naomi says when Leader asks her why. Then study the Read Like a Writer sentence, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

This is the last week of How I Became a Ghost. In Chapter 28, the wolf comes back, and Naomi has to choose in a moment. This week you also set the novel beside real history. Start noticing what only a story can tell you.

This week's words are the ones a historian uses with care: claim, evidence, reasoning, treaty, removal, nation. Then formal style, the way an essay talks. In the game, peel the husks off a long word to find the base word inside.
Three questions about Chapter 29. Then draft your source comparison paragraph. Use formal style, and begin each piece of evidence with a source transition, so your reader knows where it came from.

Read Chapter 29 in your book. It is short. Notice how the families end the day, and who promises to return. Then write a sentence shaped like the one in the Read Like a Writer box, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

Chapter 29 is the last chapter. Read it closely and mark the moments you would want to check against a real record. Today's poem was written in eighteen thirty-four. That makes the poem itself a piece of history.
Today, decide what each history word really claims. Then tell formal writing from casual talk, and sort long words by the part at their center. Three new ears of corn are waiting in the game.

Three questions about the novel and the sources. Then revise your draft with the checklist: formal style, two source transitions, a claim with evidence and reasoning, and every fact tied to its source.

Read the two sources slowly. They are short, and the plain words under each one will help. Keep the story and the record apart: the novel says eighteen thirty, and the treaty sets the removal for eighteen thirty-one to eighteen thirty-three.

The novel is finished. Today you read two real sources from the years of the Choctaw removal: part of a treaty, and part of a letter by a Choctaw chief. Ask of each one: who wrote this, when, and why?
Put the history words to work: primary source, secondary source, perspective, bias. Then practice naming your source before every claim. In the game, look for the part that can stand alone as a word.
Write your claim, then your final source comparison paragraph, formal and complete. Last, tell what a story told by a ghost taught you about real history. Copy your work and paste it into Canvas.
Reread the two sources, then look back through Chapters 28 and 29. Choose one moment from the novel and one line from a source to set side by side. Then try the Read Like a Writer box on your own.
Last day of the unit. Today's poem imagines a Native speaker, but a white poet wrote it. Set it beside the letter a Choctaw chief wrote for himself, and ask which one you would trust, and for what.
One last time: say why the exact word matters when you write about history. Keep the novel and the record apart in every sentence. Then open the last three ears of corn.

Read the opening of Chapter 29 out loud. The first paragraph is good news, so let it arrive calmly. Then let Naomi and her mother sound like two different people. When it sounds smooth, record yourself.
